summary: Describes new features for the WHOIS information lookup service, extending it beyond the original simple form. It is informational.

eli5.summary: The Internet's who is that lookup got upgrades so it can answer more kinds of questions.

subtitle: Standardized protocol for network directory lookup with advanced search and filtering

tldr.problem: The original WHOIS service was simple and limited, with no standard for record formats or search capabilities, leading to inconsistent results across different servers and forcing users to manually handle different interfaces.
tldr.mechanism: Whois++ defines standard record types for people, hosts, and domains; specifies consistent search options including exact match, wildcard, fuzzy, and range searches; and requires servers to return consistent, case-insensitive results with helpful context.
tldr.outcome: Distributed directory services became predictable and usable across the network, with clients able to narrow searches using handles and servers providing multi-level response detail and context-sensitive help.

today: RFC 1834 is an Informational document. Modern WHOIS service has evolved with WHOIS++ concepts as a foundation, though contemporary systems use a mix of WHOIS, RDAP (RESTful Directory Access Protocol), and specialized APIs for directory lookups across domain registries and network registries.

sections.title: From Simple to Standardized
sections.content:
The original NICNAME/WHOIS service, defined in RFC 954, was a simple TCP query-response database run by the Network Information Center. As networks grew, many sites created their own local directory servers for employees, hosts, and services. Each site designed them differently: different data fields, different search schemes, different response formats. The Whois and Network Information Lookup Service (WNILS) working group created Whois++ to bring consistency.

Whois++ maintains the client-server architecture but standardizes what can be searched and what will be returned. The protocol itself says nothing about how clients must be built, only that they must format queries properly and handle paged responses from servers.
sections.eli5: Many offices started keeping their own phone books with different formats. Whois++ made them all speak the same language so one tool works everywhere.

sections.title: Three Record Types with Standard Fields
sections.content:
Whois++ defines three types of records. Individual records describe people and include name, organization, title, department, email, phone, postal address, and a unique handle for disambiguation. Host records describe network-connected machines with hostname, IP address, system administrator contact information, machine type, operating system, mail exchanger, and location of additional information. Domain records describe registered domains with domain name, network address, administrative contact, technical contact, nameservers, and last update date.

Each record type has required fields and optional fields. For example, an individual must have a name and organization but may have email or phone. Every record must have a unique handle—like SMITH1, SMITH2—to distinguish multiple people with the same name.
sections.eli5: All records follow the same outline: people have name and job info, computers have name and IP address, and domains have contacts and nameservers. Every record gets a unique ID so searches can narrow down to just one match.

sections.title: Flexible and Powerful Search
sections.content:
Whois++ supports many search styles. A simple whois smith does an exact match on last name. Searches can narrow by first name with whois smith,j. Wildcards let users search whois smith* for all last names starting with Smith, or use whois smith?? to find Smith plus up to two letters. Fuzzy matching searches for names that sound like or are spelled similarly to the query. Exact handle lookup like whois !SMITH1 goes straight to one record.

For systems, queries can search by hostname (whois hamlet.ucdavis.edu), by IP address (whois 128.120.2.9, which returns a reverse lookup), or for domains using special keywords like whois domain ucdavis.edu. The server completes any query containing keywords and returns results; if no keywords are specified, the server infers the query type from context, and may automatically retry with a "begin" search if the first attempt finds no matches.
sections.eli5: Search like you naturally would: exact names, partial names with wildcards, fuzzy matching for close spellings, or an exact ID to get one match. For machines and domains, use the hostname or IP or domain name and the server figures out what you want.

sections.title: Context-Aware Responses and Help
sections.content:
Whois++ servers must return results with context and appropriate detail. When a query matches multiple records, the server returns a short-form entry for each. A single match gets the long-form with all available details. A query with zero matches triggers context-sensitive help explaining how to broaden the search (try beginning match, use wildcards, check spelling). When a search returns more than 50 matches, the server warns the user to narrow the search and offers the choice to re-specify or receive all results.

Queries yielding many results also teach the user about handles: explain that each record has a unique handle and searching for a handle will return just that record. Both clients and servers must provide help: a two-line minimal help with every response, detailed help on request, and special help handling for zero and many-result cases.
sections.eli5: The server is smart about helping. No results? It tells you how to search better. Too many results? It shows you how to narrow down with handles. One result? You get the full details.

sections.title: Room for Growth
sections.content: Whois++ acknowledges that different sites may want to store and search other kinds of information beyond the three core record types. The RFC includes mechanisms for clients to discover what extended records exist and to query for fields not defined in the standard. Sites can extend the protocol while remaining compatible with standard queries, and clients can discover and use these extensions to maximize the usefulness of the service across heterogeneous networks.
sections.eli5: While everyone agrees on basic record types, local offices can add their own special fields and record types. Clients can discover what extras are available and use them.
